Abstract: This paper proposes a multi-stage AIoT pipeline for identifying working and non-working conditions indoors from indoor environment sensor readings. Abstract: Building sensor anomaly detection is crucial for operational efficiency and equipment reliability, yet standardized evaluation frameworks are lacking, leading to inconsistent method selection. This paper presents a comprehensive comparison of anomaly detection methods using a novel unsupervised evaluation framework that incorporates statistical consistency, temporal coherence, cross-method agreement, and domain logic compliance. We evaluate three paradigms—statistical (STL), machine learning (Isolation Forest), and deep learning (LSTM Autoencoder)—on real-world building sensor data spanning two years with eight sensor types. Our results show that Isolation Forest achieves the best overall performance with a total score of 0.464 and superior computational efficiency of 0.339 seconds, detecting four collective anomalies with excellent temporal coherence. Surprisingly, the LSTM Autoencoder achieves only a 0.263 total score despite 206.444 seconds training time, challenging assumptions about deep learning superiority. These findings demonstrate that well-designed traditional methods can outperform complex deep learning approaches when considering computational efficiency and practical deployment requirements, providing essential guidance for building monitoring system design.

Abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) deployments on rural farms, in off-grid installations, and at remote monitoring stations face a critical challenge: sensor faults often go undetected due to a lack of technical expertise and cloud connectivity. This paper presents a fully offline, edge-deployable framework that (i) generates physics-based synthetic sensor data to model normal operation and three fault modes: out-of-range readings, sensor drift, and missing data; (ii) trains four lightweight machine learning (ML) classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost, and a compact multilayer perceptron) on this synthetic data and exports them via the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) format; (iii) benchmarks inference on Raspberry Pi 5 and NVIDIA Jetson AGX; and (iv) integrates an offline small language model (SLM) running locally via Ollama to translate fault classifications into plain-language diagnostics that non-technical users can act upon. Abstract: Human activity recognition poses a significant challenge within active and assisted living (AAL) systems, relying extensively on ubiquitous environmental sensor-based acquisition devices to detect user situations in their daily living.
